title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
formal:
Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family? With the definitions below, the proposition is
\[
\bigl[\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)\bigr]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl[\exists g\;\mathrm{OWF}(g)\land\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\bigr].
\]
Both sides require security against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family. The conclusion asks for the existence of some such \(g\), with some constant depth and some polynomial bounds. These constants may depend on \(g\), but not on its input length or on an adversary. There is no additional assumption on the starting function's circuit depth, no requirement that \(f\) and \(g\) have the same input or output lengths, and no requirement of a black-box construction or an efficient compiler from descriptions of \(f\).
definitions:
A candidate function is a family \(f=(f_n)_{n\ge1}\), with a length function \(m_f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\) and total maps
\[
f_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m_f(n)}.
\]
The output length depends only on \(n\), and zero is an allowed length. Let \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) mean that there are a single deterministic machine \(M\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), the machine outputs exactly \(f_n(x)\) and halts within \(B(n+1)^k\) steps, with \(m_f(n)\le B(n+1)^k\). The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finitely many tapes, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary symbols, a separator and a blank, and one-cell head moves; each transition counts as one step. The input is the binary string on a read-only input tape with end markers, work tapes are initially blank, and output bits are written sequentially on an output tape. This fixes ordinary bit computation; the number of tapes, alphabet and program are fixed independently of \(n\). No advice, oracle or random coins are supplied to the evaluator.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose input nodes carry the input bits, whose constant nodes carry \(0\) or \(1\), and whose internal gates are binary AND, binary OR or unary NOT. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same predecessor may occupy both input positions. Outputs are an ordered list of references to nodes, with repetitions allowed. Size is the number of nodes plus the number of output positions. Depth is the largest number of internal gates on a path from an input or constant node to an output. Circuit descriptions list the nodes in a topological order, with gate tags and predecessor indices, followed by the output indices; indices and list lengths are in binary with separators from a fixed finite alphabet. No gates for arbitrary functions or oracle evaluation are present.

For a candidate \(f\), an allowed inverter is any family \(A=(A_n)_{n\ge1}\) of Boolean circuits of this basis, together with integers \(r(n)\ge0\), such that
\[
A_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m_f(n)+r(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n},
\qquad
\exists C,c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,
\quad\max\{\operatorname{size}(A_n),r(n)\}\le C(n+1)^c.
\]
No uniform procedure for producing \(A_n\) is required, and its depth is unrestricted. The input blocks are \(1^n\), a proposed function value, and \(r(n)\) independent fair random bits. Thus the security parameter is given in unary, the adversary may depend on the input length nonuniformly, and it is not restricted to shallow circuits. For independent uniform strings \(X\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r(n)}\), put
\[
s_{f,A}(n)=\Pr\!\left[
f_n\bigl(A_n(1^n,f_n(X),R)\bigr)=f_n(X)
\right].
\]
Success means finding any preimage of the specified length \(n\), not necessarily the sampled \(X\). The function itself is deterministic; the probability is only over \(X\) and the adversary's coins \(R\). The negligible-success requirement is
\[
\forall A\text{ allowed}\ \forall a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists N\ge2\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad s_{f,A}(n)\le n^{-a}.
\]
The threshold \(N\) may depend on \(f,A,a\). Define \(\mathrm{OWF}(f)\) to mean \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) together with this requirement. Security holds at every sufficiently large length for each adversary and exponent, rather than merely on infinitely many lengths. There is no requirement of injectivity, length preservation, expansion, or any fixed ratio of output to input length.

The predicate \(\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\) means that there are a single deterministic circuit-generating Turing machine \(G\), integers \(B,k\ge1\), and an integer \(D\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\), the machine \(G\) outputs the full description of a circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(B(n+1)^k\) steps. That circuit has exactly \(n\) input bits, exactly \(m_g(n)\) outputs, size at most \(B(n+1)^k\), and depth at most \(D\), and satisfies \(C_n(x)=g_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). Generation uses the same deterministic bit-computation convention as above. The depth bound is a single constant for the entire family; in particular, every output depends on at most \(2^D\) input bits. The question places no bound on how many outputs a given input bit may influence. Circuit generation has no random setup, randomly chosen graph, public key or advice. The two existentially quantified functions may have different length functions and polynomial bounds.

context_blocks.text: Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz explicitly ask whether an arbitrary one-way function implies a one-way function in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\). A local function can expose many output bits, each depending on only a constant number of inputs, while inversion must remain difficult for general polynomial-size circuits.

Their theorems establish the implication when the starting one-way function has a polynomial-time uniform nondeterministic branching-program representation of polynomial size, which in particular covers logspace and uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

This card retains its existing editorial choices of deterministic polynomial-time uniform evaluation, length-dependent output size, same-length preimages, and nonuniform circuit security; the source uses polynomial-time uniformity by default and explicitly extends its security results to nonuniform adversaries.

The Ren–Santhanam revision of August 2025 still explicitly describes the general implication as open and gives a characterization through average-case Kolmogorov complexity in its stated uniform-adversary setting.

why: The question tests whether the minimal computational assumption underlying much of cryptography already guarantees functions with constant-depth local evaluation. A positive answer would make this extreme parallelism available under the general one-way-function assumption; a negative answer would separate local cryptographic hardness from unrestricted polynomial-time cryptographic hardness.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed implication or of its logical negation, using exactly the evaluation, uniformity and nonuniform-security conventions above. A positive proof must establish the existence of a secure family with one constant depth bound from the sole assumption that a one-way function exists. A negative proof must establish both
\[
\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall g,\quad\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\Longrightarrow\neg\mathrm{OWF}(g).
\]
Equivalently, for every candidate \(g\) with such a uniform constant-depth implementation, it must establish an allowed polynomial-size inverter family \(A\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) with
\[
\forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N,\qquad s_{g,A}(n)>n^{-a},
\]
as well as the existence of an unrestricted one-way function. The inverter and exponent may depend on \(g\). A separation only relative to an oracle, an obstruction only to a selected kind of reduction, or failure of a particular local candidate does not prove this negation. A theorem under an additional computational assumption establishes only that conditional result.

progress.text: Applebaum, Ishai and Kushilevitz show that a one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size nondeterministic branching programs implies a one-way function with output locality four. Their general open question allows any constant output locality and starts from an arbitrary polynomial-time one-way function.

The Mao–Mazor–Zhang revision gives non-adaptive constructions of universal one-way hash functions from arbitrary one-way functions. Its constant-depth corollary still assumes that a one-way function exists in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\); treating oracle calls as gates does not remove that hypothesis.

Ren and Santhanam retain the general question in their revised introduction, alongside their characterization of local one-way functions by average-case hardness of \(\mathrm{KT}\) complexity. Their separate characterization of unrestricted one-way functions uses a different time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity measure, so these results do not establish the displayed implication.

status_note: The general implication is explicit in AIK’s 2006 open questions and is still described as open in Ren–Santhanam’s ECCC revision of 25 August 2025. This card retains its declared P-uniform evaluation and nonuniform circuit-security conventions; AIK explicitly supports the latter extension, whereas the later paper states its main definitions using PPT adversaries. Individual primary-source reading and bounded subsequent checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is a dated source-open assessment, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

sentences: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but resists inversion on a uniformly chosen input by every polynomial-size adversary.
The question asks whether the existence of any such function guarantees one whose Boolean circuits have a single constant depth bound.
The circuits must be generated deterministically in polynomial time, while inversion security is required against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuits.
Known theorems establish this implication under restricted computational assumptions, and a 2025 source still explicitly lists the general implication as open.
A complete Lean proof must establish the implication or prove both that general one-way functions exist and that every eligible local family is insecure.
